summary: Proposes a new top-level MIME content type called model, to extend the types defined in the first MIME document, so email can carry things like 3D models.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2077 adds a MIME primary type called model for three-dimensional models, such as CAD drawings and simulation meshes. It groups the formats that describe models under one label, so a mail program knows the data is a model and not an image or a sound file.

questions: what is the mime model type
how to send 3d models by email
how are unknown model subtypes handled
how are model subtypes handled when unknown
subtitle: A MIME primary type for three-dimensional models, so CAD and simulation files travel with their meaning intact.

tldr.problem: Three-dimensional models travel over the Internet in several unrelated formats, and a receiver cannot tell from the file itself how to interpret them. Sending a CAD drawing as an image or an audio file destroys information the sender meant to keep.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a new MIME primary type called model, with subtypes for the formats that describe models, plus optional parameters that name the dimensionality and whether the data is static or dynamic.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2077 is a Proposed Standard from January 1997 and has been updated by RFC 9141. It registers the model type as the parent for subtypes such as model/iges, model/vrml and model/mesh.

today: RFC 2077 is a Proposed Standard from January 1997 and has been updated by RFC 9141. The type it registers, model, remains the parent for the model subtypes that carry CAD, VRML and mesh data.

sections.title: Overview and Purpose
sections.content:
The RFC states its aim plainly: it outlines what a model is, shows examples of models and explains the benefit of grouping them together. It does not register the individual subtypes, because each of those has its own registration document.

The document is written as a discussion paper for an agreed definition, intended to become a standard extension to RFC 2045, the MIME specification that defines the format of Internet message bodies. The intended readers are developers of input and output filters, of viewer software and of hardware, plus people who build MIME transport and decoding software.

Because a model is a new primary type rather than a new subtype, mail programs can react to it as a class: a program that has never seen a particular model subtype can still apply the general rules for models.
sections.plainLanguage: The document defines one new MIME type, called model, and leaves the individual formats to separate registrations. Its readers are the people who write mail programs, viewers and filters that have to recognise model data.

sections.title: The Definition of a Model
sections.content:
A model is an electronically exchangeable behavioural or physical representation within a given domain. The RFC summarises it as a multidimensional structure made of one or more objects, where one object defines the arrangement and relationship of the others, and where the objects have calibrated coordinate systems that need not use the same units or the same dimensionality.

Four properties set models apart from other kinds of data. First, a model has three or more dimensions formed by a set of basis functions over a coordinate system, and any orthogonal system will do, so skewed systems and elliptical coordinates are allowed. Second, the model elements have a structural relationship to one another. Third, the model carries scaling or calibration factors tied to physical units such as force, momentum, time, velocity, acceleration and size, so that an IGES file can describe a building of a definite size and a VRML model can have real spatial and temporal units. Fourth, a model may be a single object or a collection of objects arranged so that one acts as the reference for the others.

The RFC draws the distinction between data that describes how something behaves and data that describes how something is. The collection of objects works like the multipart/related content type in mail, which defines how the parts relate, and the subtype authors are left to specify it further.
sections.plainLanguage: A model is a multidimensional description with a relationship between its parts, physical units attached to it, and often several objects where one sets the position of the others. The types grouped here describe how something behaves, not just what it is.

sections.title: Consultation Mechanisms
sections.content:
Before proposing a subtype for the model type, the RFC asks the author to read the definition of what a model is and to look at the list of what a model is not. It also suggests consulting the authors of the model subtypes that already exist, since a new subtype should fit the family rather than duplicate part of it.

The RFC points readers at the archived VRML discussion list and at the comp.mail.mime group, and notes that discussion digests for the existing model subtypes are referenced in the documents that register them. It also points out a problem in the mesh community: many different mesh geometries exist in different packages, so the author asks that freely available libraries be advertised, so that interoperable packages can develop.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC sets out how to propose a new model subtype: read the definition, check what already exists and talk to the authors of the existing subtypes. It also points out that mesh formats need shared libraries to be usable together.

sections.title: Media Type Name, Parameters and Encoding
sections.content:
The registration follows the usual MIME pattern. The media type name is model, the subtype name follows, no parameters are required, and two optional parameters are defined: dimensionality, a number giving the number of dimensions, and state, which is either static or dynamic. The dimensionality is a hint that helps choose a suitable viewer program. The state says whether the observer may move around the data without changing it, or whether the data itself is manipulated, for example by skewing or scaling. The RFC notes that time evolution still counts as static, because it is a translation along one of the principal dimensions.

On encoding, a subtype of model that a program does not recognise should at least be treated as application/octet-stream, and a program may instead pass it to a general-purpose model viewer if one is available. Unless a subtype's own registration says otherwise, model subtypes are assumed to hold binary data, which means base64 content encoding for mail and binary transfer for file and web transfers.

The RFC shows a sample header for a mesh file sent by mail, with the content type set to model/mesh and the two optional parameters filled in, and the body following as base64 text.
sections.plainLanguage: The type name is model, with two optional parameters: how many dimensions the data has, and whether it is static or dynamic. Unrecognised model subtypes are handled as ordinary binary data, and mail carries them as base64.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that model data files are read-only and contain no file system modifiers and no batch or macro commands. The data does not modify itself, but it may contain interrelationships between elements.

One file feature does need care. A model file may contain a default view, added by the author when the file was created, that sets viewer variables such as the default look angle, the lighting and the visualisation options. Computing those values from the raw data can change the state of the equipment, and for motorized equipment it can move the object from its rest position to its starting orientation.

The internal structure of a model file may also direct an agent to fetch further data from the network. The RFC does not set security limits for who may be reached this way and leaves those actions to the security rules of the inclusions themselves. Comments about subtypes are left to each subtype's own registration.
sections.plainLanguage: Model files are read-only and cannot run commands, but a file can set the default view, which may move motorized equipment into a starting position. A file can also point at more data to fetch from the network.

sections.title: Expected Subtypes
sections.content:
The RFC lists three subtypes that are expected to exist, with suggested file extensions for DOS compatibility, and it does not register them itself. The IGES type is registered today as application/iges, and one of the authors of that registration is an author of this document, so it will be re-registered as model/iges in due course. The VRML type is described as gaining wide acceptance, and the mesh type is an offshoot of existing computational meshing work. Most modern meshes are derived from CAD solid files.

The appendices add background on the three families. The VRML format is becoming a standard for displaying 3D information on the web. Mesh files come from finite element and finite difference time domain codes, and are made of many simple objects with an implicit connectivity and neighbour list, where a mesh of a million elements is small and a hundred million element structured mesh is large. IGES, the Initial Graphics Exchange Specification, is a neutral data format that lets CAD systems from different vendors exchange product data, and it was adopted as an American National Standard in November 1981.
sections.plainLanguage: Three subtypes are expected: IGES for CAD data, VRML for 3D scenes on the web, and mesh for simulation data. The RFC lists them for guidance and leaves their registration to separate documents.

viz.caption: THE FOUR PROPERTIES THAT DEFINE A MODEL

items.title: Three or more dimensions
items.text: Built from a set of basis functions over a coordinate system. Any orthogonal system is acceptable.

items.title: Structural relationship
items.text: The elements of the model relate to one another, not just to the coordinate system.

items.title: Physical units
items.text: Scaling and calibration factors refer to force, time, velocity, size and similar units.

items.title: One or more objects
items.text: A model may be a single object, or a set in which one object is the reference for the others.

viz.caption: THE EXAMPLE MAIL HEADER FROM SECTION 4 OF RFC 2077

data.title: A mesh model sent by mail
data.code:
To:   you@some.org
From: nelson18@llnl.gov
Date: Fri, 30 Aug 96 13:33:19 -0700
Content-Type: model/mesh; dimension="4"; state="static"
Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64
MIME-Version: 1.0
Subject: model data file

viz.caption: THE EXPECTED MODEL SUBTYPES AND THEIR FILE EXTENSIONS

items.label: igs, iges
items.desc: IGES CAD data. Already registered as application/iges and to be re-registered.

items.label: wrl
items.desc: Virtual Reality Modeling Language scenes for 3D display on the web.

items.label: msh, mesh, silo
items.desc: Computational meshes with geometry and results data. The silo extension is for backwards compatibility.
